titleDv: ގޭންގުތަކުން ހިންގާ ކުށްތަކާއި އިންތިޒާމުވެގެން ނުރައްކާތެރި ކުށްތައް ހުއްޓުވުމުގެ ބިލު
summary: This is a new law from the government on gang crimes, organised serious crime and violent crimes involving weapons. It defines an organised criminal group as three or more people working together to commit serious crimes for money or other gain, and makes it a crime to form, run, recruit for, join, support or show membership of such a group, including displaying a gang symbol or tattoo. It sets long prison terms for knife and weapon attacks, gives police extra powers to search, arrest, run undercover operations and freeze or confiscate property, and lets courts put young people and suspected adult gang members under control orders. It would repeal Law No. 17/2010 (on threats and carrying dangerous weapons and sharp objects) and Law No. 18/2010 (on prohibiting gang crimes).
whyItMatters: Showing a gang symbol could carry up to 12 years in prison, people suspected of these crimes would not get bail and could be kept from a private meeting with a lawyer for up to 48 hours, and property could be confiscated even without a conviction. Adults and 15 to 18 year olds linked to gangs could face court orders limiting where they go, who they meet and how they use the internet, including GPS tags for adults.
keyProvisions: Articles 17 to 22 create the group offences: forming or running an organised criminal group carries 25 years and a fine of MVR 200,000 to 10 million; recruiting carries 20 years (25 if a child is recruited); taking part carries 15 years; showing membership or displaying the group's symbol carries 12 years; seeking support for a group carries 10 years. Article 25 lets courts fine a company MVR 1 million to 100 million and order it dissolved.

Articles 26 to 29 make it a crime for someone linked to such a group to hold wealth out of proportion to their lawful income that they cannot explain, with a fine of MVR 500,000 to 1 million; the Prosecutor General can ask a court to declare the wealth unlawful.

Article 30 covers crimes committed with a sharp object or dangerous weapon: intentional killing carries the death penalty (life in prison if the victim's heirs forgive), serious assault 20 years, kidnapping 15 years and threats 10 years. Carrying a weapon in public without a valid reason carries 12 years (Article 31), importing flick or butterfly knives without a permit is banned (Articles 33 and 37), and selling any knife to a child is fined MVR 20,000 to 100,000 (Article 34).

Articles 38 to 48 let police search and arrest suspects without a court order in some cases, stop and search vessels, and run controlled deliveries and undercover operations with senior police approval; police must report the numbers of these operations to the Majlis security services committee each year.

Articles 49 to 53 let courts freeze and confiscate money and property linked to these crimes, including without a conviction if the person has a criminal record and cannot show it was lawfully obtained (judged on the civil standard); private access to a lawyer can be delayed up to 48 hours, and suspects of these crimes have no right to bail.

Articles 54 to 80 allow High Court orders for 15 to 18 year olds involved in gang violence or drug trade (up to 2 years) and monitoring and control orders for suspected adult members (up to 1 year, extendable by 1 more year), which can limit movement, travel, contacts and transactions and require GPS tags. Breaking a control order carries up to 18 months in prison. The law would take effect 3 months after it is published in the gazette.
whoIsAffected: People involved in or suspected of links to gangs and violent crime, young people aged 15 to 18, shops that sell knives, and the police, Prosecutor General and courts who would use the new powers.
statedReasons: The explanatory note says the bill sets up a detailed legal framework to protect the public and society from gang crimes and organised dangerous crimes that create fear among ordinary people, by defining offences and penalties, giving law enforcement special powers, setting rules to keep offenders and young people away from crime and help them return to society, and setting rules for monitoring people who commit such crimes.
